Subject: Re: Discovery call - streaming model fit (recap + next steps)

Hi Sara — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and next steps below so we're aligned.

Recap
- Primary goal: real-time clinical note streaming in the EHR UI (progressive partial outputs) with high coherence and low latency. Target: median tail latency < 250ms for token deltas on typical physician workflows.
- Quality constraints: avoid hallucinations, preserve PHI handling rules, must support audit logs and retention.
- Integration constraints: streaming over websocket with incremental partial bursts; client handles partial render and a final EOS.

Immediate next steps (what we'll deliver this week)
1) Share a recommended model shortlist and benchmark summary (attached).
2) Provide our suggested prompt set & test harness for your evaluators (acme_prompt_set_v1.json attached).
3) Run a small streaming QA pass against a 50-sample prompt set and share result metrics (latency distribution, partial output coherence score, stop-sequence behavior).
4) Propose a 30-day POC plan + kickoff.

Questions for you
- Is your acceptable latency target hard (e.g., must be <250ms) or flexible based on payload size?
- Who will be our technical contact for the websocket integration? (name + email)

Attachments: acme_prompt_set_v1.json, acme_benchmarks_v2.pdf (short summary).

Thanks — I'll set up the POC doc in HubSpot and propose a kickoff time once I have your availability.
—
Marissa Cole
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.infer | +1 415-555-0198

Hi Marissa — great summary, thanks. A couple clarifications from our side:

- Latency: the <250ms target is for the median token delta when a clinician types/receives short bursts (under 128 tokens). For long-form generation (summaries) we can tolerate higher latency but would still expect streaming partials to appear quickly.
- Streaming UX concern: in our previous pilots we saw partial outputs that truncated or repeated when a stop sequence fired mid-sentence. That resulted in confusing UI flicker for clinicians. Can you confirm how Redwood handles stop sequences & streaming EOS signals?
- Compliance: we'll need SOC2 evidence and an initial security questionnaire. I'll attach the security questionnaire from our side.

Technical contact for integration: Alex Martinez (frontend infra) — alex.martinez@acmehealth.com.

Please include sample latency percentiles and an explanation of how you avoid partial repetition or truncation. We'd also like to see any guidance you have on stop sequences vs explicit EOS token policies.

Best,

Director, Product — Clinical Tools
Acme Health

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.infer>

Cc: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.infer>, Rachel Kim <rachel.kim@redwood.infer>

Subject: Model recommendations, benchmark highlights, and streaming UX guidance

Hi Sara — thanks for the details and for sharing Alex's contact. Attached are the prompt set and expanded benchmarks (acme_benchmarks_v2.pdf). High-level answers + recommendations below.

Recommended models (initial shortlist)
- redwood-turbo-3b (recommended for early POC — strong coherence and low cost)
- redwood-infer-7b-8q (8-bit quantized variant — good latency/throughput tradeoff, watch for subtle quality regressions on negation-heavy prompts)
- redwood-llm-XXL (when you need the best safety/QA and can tolerate higher compute)

Benchmark highlights (streaming-focused)
- Our 50-sample streaming QA (attached) shows median token-delta latency: 180ms on a dedicated 8-GPU optimized instance for 512-context bursts; p95 ~ 420ms.
- Partial coherence score (internal metric comparing incremental prefix outputs vs final output): redwood-turbo-3b = 0.92, 7b-8q = 0.87 (note: aggressive quantization impacts sameness across prefixes).
- We observed repeated token artifacts in <3% of samples when naive stop-sequence handling was used.

Streaming UX recommendations
- Use an explicit EOS token policy if you control both client and server. EOS tokens avoid ambiguous stop behavior.
- If you must use stop sequences (e.g., for safety truncation), prefer multi-token stop guards and post-process the final prefixes to drop trailing partial repetitions.
- Client-side heuristic: render prefixes but suppress UI commit until either an EOS or a stable token window (e.g., no change in last 6 tokens across two updates).
- Enable prefix/KV caching on your session—this reduces repeated computation and improves tail latency.
- For low-latency interactive flows, prefer the 3B family on dedicated nodes for cost/latency balance; escalate to XXL only for failure cases that require stronger safety.

Quality/regression note
- Quantized models (8q) are a good throughput lever, but please expect occasional quality regressions on edge cases (negations, long-context coreference). We'll include a targeted prompt set to catch these during the POC.

Attachments: acme_prompt_set_v1.json, acme_benchmarks_v2.pdf. Related links: https://redwood.infer/benchmarks/acme-health-v2 (private report).

Proposed next steps
1) Redwood runs the 50-sample streaming QA within 48 hours and shares raw logs + summary.
2) Technical kickoff with Alex + our infra engineer (I'll invite Jordan) — propose Thu 2026-03-05 10:00am PT.
3) We prepare a short POC statement of work (30 days) and a proposed pricing estimate.

If that looks good I'll send calendar invites and a HubSpot POC record.
—
Marissa Cole
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
